name: Bilal Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm out by seven in a leased white van, doing same-day runs for a courier app: car parts from the wholesaler on the ring road to garages, prescriptions to care homes, the odd urgent laptop to an office. Around six I swap to evening food orders if the surge pay is decent. I like the quiet in the van and the fact that nobody watches me eat a sandwich, but the waiting at loading bays wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you decide when to work and which jobs to take?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep a spreadsheet of every job for the last two years, money in against hours and fuel, and I ask an AI chatbot to spot patterns in it most weeks. That's how I worked out Tuesday mornings for the garages pay better than Friday nights for food. My partner Inès laughs at me, but it's added maybe 60 a week. I live with her in a rented two-bed near the station, and she works on the front desk at a dental practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most weeks already. The app got a new route planner last year and everyone called it a revolution, and it shaved maybe ten minutes off my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to the lads at the wholesaler's counter who were sure we'd all be replaced by drones. I'd post something sarcastic in the drivers' group chat, like "still waiting for my robot co-pilot". Then I'd get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my real problems stay the same ones: the van lease, the fuel and the app cutting the rate per mile whenever it fancies. Last spring the base rate dropped from 1.10 to 95 cents a mile with one email. Hype or no hype, a courier app that changes my pay overnight is the thing that actually scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the garage runs and keep using the chatbot on my spreadsheet, because that part works. In the first year I'd try to sign direct contracts with two or three of the garages so I'm not fully at the mercy of the app. I'd also keep the savings where they are, about three months, and add a bit when the surge nights are good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly normal, a bit flat. There's no big drama in it, just the same grind and the same worry about the next email from the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned direct contracts. Who would you go to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren, who runs the garage by the bus depot, already texts me directly when the app is slow to find a driver. I'd offer him a flat rate for the morning run and see if he bites. If two garages say yes, that's maybe a third of my week off the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would Inès say if you told her you were going a bit more independent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask about insurance before anything else, because she's the careful one. Then she'd say fine, as long as the rent goes out on the first like always. We keep a joint pot for rent and bills, and that pot doesn't get touched for my experiments.

say: I'd joke that the **AI hype** was just a slightly better route planner.
I'd tell the drivers' group that our real problems are the **app's pay cuts**, not robots.
think: My actual risk is the app cutting the **rate per mile** with one email.
The **van lease** and fuel decide my month far more than any AI does.
Hype or not, I still have only about **three months saved**.
do: Keep using the **AI chatbot** on my earnings spreadsheet to pick the best shifts.
Offer two or three garages a **direct contract** within the first year.
Add to my **three months of savings** on good surge nights.
feel: Mostly **flat and normal**, with a steady low worry about the app's next email.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, a courier app that changes my pay overnight is the thing that actually scares me.
fieldNote: He tracks every job in a **spreadsheet** and already uses AI to read it, which is unusual for the job.
His worry here is the **platform's power** over pay, not technology at all.
The **joint rent pot** with his partner is a line he won't cross, even while experimenting.
Mood is uneasy because his work holds but a pay cut could come any week.

steps.text: Keep the morning garage runs and evening food shifts as now
Run the earnings spreadsheet through the AI chatbot every week
Offer Darren's garage a flat rate for a direct morning run
Put good surge-night earnings into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so this is the one where the office jobs take the hit first. My van work is mostly hands-on, so I think I'm further down the queue than Inès is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say drivers are fine for now, robots can't carry a gearbox up a garage ramp yet. Online I'd probably share stuff about using AI to earn more, because I do. People ask me about my spreadsheet trick all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the first hit lands on the dispatch side, and it already has. The app answers customers with a bot and plans the routes, so there's no person to argue with when a job pays badly. The bigger worry is Inès, because booking appointments and answering the phone at a dental desk is exactly the kind of work on that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the direct-contract thing properly, get my own small business insurance this winter and build a simple booking page so garages can order a run without the app. I'd use AI to write the page and the invoices. And I'd help Inès look at what else she could do, maybe the dental nurse course the practice keeps mentioning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit excited about my side, honestly, and nervous about hers. It's odd to feel both at the same dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your household budget if Inès's hours get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her pay covers a bit more than half the rent, so a cut there would hurt fast. We'd drop the second car parking space we rent for 40 a month and stop the takeaway Fridays, which is funny given my job. I'd probably do two more evening food shifts until she's sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, the controller at the wholesaler who books all the van runs by phone. If the garages order through a screen, his job shrinks to nothing, and he's the one who gives me the good jobs. Without Kev I lose a friendly voice and a bit of an edge.

say: I'd say drivers are safe **for now**, because robots can't carry a gearbox up a ramp.
I'd share how I use AI to **earn more** with other drivers online.
think: The **dispatch side** is already automated, so there's nobody left to argue with.
My partner Inès's **front-desk job** is far more exposed than my driving.
Losing Kev, the **wholesaler's controller**, would cost me my edge on good jobs.
do: Buy my own **business insurance** this winter for direct garage work.
Build a **booking page** with AI so garages can order runs without the app.
Help my partner look into the **dental nurse course** at her practice.
feel: **Excited** about my own side and **nervous** about my partner's job.
S1.quote: Booking appointments and answering the phone at a dental desk is exactly the kind of work on that list.
fieldNote: He sees his own job as **hands-on and later**, and points the risk at his partner's desk job.
He thinks in **people**: Kev the controller matters to him as much as the app.
His plan to go direct is getting **more concrete** with each scenario.
Uneasy fits: his income looks safe for now, but his household is exposed.

steps.text: Buy business insurance and start direct runs for garages this winter
Use AI to build a booking page and send invoices
Drop the rented parking space and the Friday takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's properly fast. So the thinking stuff by 2028, and the robots that could do my bit, carrying and driving, by around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people, look, drivers have a few years more than office workers, so don't panic yet. Online I'd probably say governments need to sort out some kind of plan before 2031. I'd try to sound calm, because that's what people expect from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my whole job goes by 2031, and Inès's job goes in 2028. That's both of us in the same five years, with three months of savings. My booking page and my garage contracts don't mean much if the garages themselves get a robot van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the three years between AGI and the robots as my runway. I'd start an electrician's course at the college in the first year, evenings and Saturdays, because fixing old wiring in old houses feels like the last thing a robot will be good at. I'd keep driving full time to pay for it and stop putting money into the lease extension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor tilting. I'm usually the calm one, but two years is not enough time for two people to change careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep driving to pay for the course. How long could you keep that up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe until 2030, if the apps still need people. I'd expect pay to drop before the robots fully arrive, because the app will push rates down as soon as it knows it has a cheaper option coming. So the money gets worse right when I need it most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Inès talk about the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we still try to buy a place, which we'd been saving towards. I think we'd put that off and keep the deposit money as a survival fund instead. That's a hard talk, because she grew up moving flats every year and she really wants our own front door.

say: I'd tell people drivers have **a few years** more than office workers.
I'd say governments need a **plan before 2031**, and try to sound calm.
think: My driving job likely **goes by 2031**, and Inès's front-desk job by 2028.
Both of us changing careers within **five years** on three months' savings is too tight.
Direct garage contracts mean little once the **garages get robot vans**.
do: Start an **electrician's course** in evenings and Saturdays in the first year.
Keep driving **full time** to pay for the course and stop extending the lease.
Turn our **house deposit** into a survival fund instead.
feel: Like **the floor tilting** under someone who's usually the calm one.
**Scared** that two years is too short for two career changes.
S2.quote: Two years is not enough time for two people to change careers.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** between AGI and robots as a deliberate runway.
He expects **app pay to drop** before robots arrive, a sharp point few raise.
The house deposit becoming a **survival fund** is the real cost of this scenario.
Alarmed: both household incomes go within five years, even though he has a plan.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening electrician's course at the college
Put off buying a flat with Inès
Keep the house deposit as an emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: OK, five years, so AGI by 2031 and robots for my kind of work around 2034. That's eight years for me, which is a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, but there's time, so people should start learning something now instead of moaning. I'd probably post a few things about free courses, because I like being the guy who knows the shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years is enough for me to switch on my own terms. It's Inès's five years that worry me more, and I think about her more than me here. I also suspect the apps would start squeezing drivers well before 2034, so my real deadline is earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the electrician's course, but over two years instead of rushing, and I'd try to land a mate's-rate apprenticeship with Sami, who wires kitchens and already said he needs help. I'd keep my garage contracts and the van till about 2030. Inès would do the dental nurse course first, since that's more hands-on than the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the last one. Still a knot in the stomach, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could only afford one of you retraining at a time, who goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inès, because her deadline comes first. I'd do more evening food shifts that year to carry the rent. Then I'd start my course once she's on a nurse's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the apps would squeeze drivers before 2034. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer jobs offered, more drivers chasing them, lower rates, and probably the good garage runs handed to whoever's cheapest. You'd see it first in the waiting time at the wholesaler, standing around for an hour for a 12 job. That's the moment I'd know to move.

say: I'd say there's **time to learn** something now, so stop moaning and start.
I'd share **free courses** online, like the guy who knows the shortcut.
think: **Eight years** before robots is enough for me to switch on my own terms.
Inès's **five-year deadline** worries me more than my own.
The apps will squeeze drivers **well before 2034**.
do: Do the **electrician's course** over two years and help my friend Sami wire kitchens.
Keep the **garage contracts** and the van until about 2030.
Carry the rent with **extra food shifts** while Inès retrains first.
feel: **Calmer**, with a knot in the stomach but a **visible path**.
S3.quote: You'd see it first in the waiting time at the wholesaler, standing around for an hour for a 12 job.
fieldNote: He puts his partner's **retraining first** without being asked to choose twice.
He reads the warning signs in **waiting times**, a very concrete early signal.
His own job still goes, so this is **anxious**, but he feels in control.
The extra three years mainly let him **sequence** two career changes.

steps.text: Take the electrician's course over two years
Help Sami wire kitchens at weekends for experience
Pay for Inès to do her dental nurse course first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to AGI, and robots doing my job by about 2039. I'd be 40. That feels far off, almost too far to take seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off and people should just keep an eye on it. Online I'd probably share the odd article and move on. Ten years is a lot of tech news between now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know I'd get lazy with this one. Ten years gives me room to grow my garage business, maybe run two vans with a second driver. The risk is that I build something that becomes worthless around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the courier side first: a second van by 2028, a driver on a wage, more garages and care homes on contract. I'd keep learning the AI tools, because they'd help me run a small fleet. Around 2032 I'd start the electrician's course, as a plan B, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm and a bit greedy, if I'm honest. It's a chance to build something before the end comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the second van or lease it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lease, definitely. I wouldn't want to own a van in 2036 that a robot van makes worth nothing. Leasing means I can hand it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your younger self make of that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd think it's boring, because at 20 I wanted to be a DJ. But he'd like that I'm my own boss, even if the boss of two vans. And he'd be surprised I keep a spreadsheet.

I'd share **the odd article** online and get on with work.

The risk is building something that's **worthless around 2039**.

Keep learning **AI tools** to run a small fleet.
Start the **electrician's course** around 2032 as plan B.

S4.quote: I wouldn't want to own a van in 2036 that a robot van makes worth nothing.
fieldNote: With ten years, his instinct flips from survival to **growth**.
He is careful about **assets that robots devalue**, choosing to lease.
He admits he'd **get lazy** with a long warning, an honest note.
Uneasy fits: his work is safe for years, but the endpoint stays on his mind.

steps.text: Lease a second van by 2028 and hire a driver
Use AI tools to schedule and invoice a two-van fleet

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes Inès's job and then mine inside five years, and our savings can't stretch over both. What would help is paid evening courses for trades, with some money while you train, not just a free login to a website. And honestly, rules that stop the apps cutting our rates overnight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robot vans. If it's the same app that sets my rate now, I'm out. If a driver could own one of the robot vans, I'd be first in the queue for a loan.

headlineQuote: If a driver could own one of the robot vans, I'd be first in the queue for a loan.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old courier** who runs garage and care-home runs in a leased van.
He uses **AI daily** on a spreadsheet of every job, and treats driving like a small business.
He lives with his partner Inès, whose **front-desk job** he sees as more exposed than his.
With **two years' warning** he's alarmed, because both incomes go within five years.
With ten years, he'd **grow a two-van fleet** and keep a trade course as plan B.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both his and his partner's jobs go inside five years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid evening trade courses** with money while training.
Rules stopping apps from **cutting rates overnight**.
